english: "The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear Him, and He will deliver them" (Psalm 33:8 [34:7]). These are the angels who guard us in the night. "Who set its measures, if you know? Or who stretched a measuring-line upon it?" (Job 38:5). The Greeks wanted to say something about the measure of the earth: the diameter of the earth, they say, is two hundred and fifty thousand stadia. But the word seems to show that the measure of the earth is incomprehensible to everyone; only the Savior knows it, He who is also its maker. He said "measures" and not "measure" to represent the differences of the earth. What is the measure of this kind of land—say, of the East that bears spices? What is the measure of the land that bears pepper or animals? For not everything grows everywhere. These measures, then, are with the Word of God. The earth has not simply become as large as it is, nor by chance, but it seems to me that if even a random amount were added, it would be out of season, and if it were taken away, by the same reasoning it would ruin the whole earth. This is what the measures and the measuring-line hint at.

"Who is it that laid a cornerstone upon it?" (Job 38:6). Who is it that laid a cornerstone upon it, so that it stands firm, as though it had been built upon a foundation that rests securely? By the will of God, for in His hand are all the ends of the earth. "Cornerstone": this can also be understood of the Only-Begotten Son of God, who for our sake became flesh, according to the psalm: "The stone which they rejected has become the head of the corner" (Psalm 117:22 [118:22]). For by the good pleasure of the Father He came to earth and joined in Himself the two peoples, Jews and Gentiles, just as a cornerstone binds together both walls.

"I said to it: You shall come this far, and you shall not go beyond" (Job 38:11). Symmachus has: "Let the swelling of your waves be ordered as far as here." For He holds it back as securely as with bars, yet as easily as by a command. "I said," He says, and there is no contradicting it, since this happens without any necessity forcing it—even though great violence and force lash at it. For this reason He did not allow it to be calm or gentle, so that it might proclaim the power of God, as nature fights against the command and the command prevails everywhere. For if the water were gentle, many would attribute its good order to the nature of water. But now, stirred up, lashed, driven from within, and unable to cross its boundaries, through its turmoil it proclaims the power of God.

"Who has prepared food for the raven?" (Job 38:41). For it is said that the raven does not feed its young; they themselves, reasonably, since they are large, provide food. But who feeds the young? Is it not the word of God? As the Gospel also says: "The birds of the air do not sow, nor do they reap, and your heavenly Father feeds them" (Matthew 6:26). "Does the eagle rise at your command? And does the vulture, sitting upon its nest, lodge on a crag of rock and in a hidden place?" (Job 39:27). If you see in the flesh-eaters a certain rational wisdom, present in each from natural knowledge and for knowledge—for some, knowledge of war; for others, knowledge of the dead—you also see the vulture borne aloft in the air.

"Why am I still judged, being admonished and reproving the Lord, hearing such things, being nothing?" (Job 39:34). "Why am I still judged," he says, "as a prelude?" And from the beginning he yielded the first place. "I am defeated," he says; "I have lost my case before You. Why do You pursue the case further? What answer is possible? How should one face such a Master?" He says: "I kept seeking the cause of the blow that came upon me; I brought no charge against creation, and against what has been said I have nothing to say." The phrase is incomplete: "as not even reproving the Lord, being admonished"—the wretched man.

"But gird up your loins like a man; I will question you, and you shall answer Me" (Job 40:2). For those who are confident in an abundance of righteous deeds do not even shun their adversaries but give them free rein, so that the victory may come out of that abundance. Then He also defends Himself to him, saying: "I care about human beings. It is clear from this why I brought this trial upon you. I give you freedom to speak; I will question you, and you shall answer Me." "Do you think that I have dealt with you for any other reason than that you might be shown righteous?" (Job 40:3). He speaks of the present dealing. "I do not say these things to condemn you," He says, "but to show you righteous." Or He speaks about the trial, calling the permission a "dealing"—that is, "I arranged beforehand for this to happen for another reason." He did not say "so that you might become," but "so that you might be shown as what you were, so that you might instruct others."
